p.src: Now the Great Immortal Zhenyuan took the Pilgrim by the arm and said, “I know your powers, and I have heard of your great fame. But this time you have defied all reason and betrayed your conscience. For all your tricks of escape, you will not get out of my hands. I will argue the matter with you all the way to the Western Heaven, and even before your Buddha you will still have to restore my ginseng-fruit tree. Do not try any magic tricks.” The Pilgrim laughed. “Master, how petty you are! If you want the tree revived, what difficulty is there in that? Had you said so earlier, would it not have spared us that whole fight?” The Great Immortal said, “Without that fight, would I ever have willingly spared you?” The Pilgrim said, “Release my master, and I will give you back a living tree. How does that sound?” The Great Immortal said, “If you truly possess such power and can heal the tree, I will exchange the eight ceremonial bows with you and become your sworn brother.” The Pilgrim said, “That is easily settled. Release them, and Old Monkey guarantees you shall have your living tree back.”

p.src: Certain that he could not escape, the Great Immortal ordered Tripitaka, Bajie, and Sha Monk to be untied and released. Sha Monk said, “Master, who knows what mischief Elder Brother is scheming now?” Bajie said, “What mischief? This is what you call ‘doing a favor to someone’s face while playing the devil behind his back.’ How can a dead tree possibly be brought back to life? He is merely putting on a fine show, pretending to go seek a cure for the tree, when all he really wants is to get away by himself. Do you think he will still care about you and me?” Tripitaka said, “He would never dare abandon us. Let us ask where he means to seek this cure.” He therefore called, “Wukong, how have you deceived the immortal master into releasing us?” The Pilgrim said, “Old Monkey spoke nothing but the honest truth. How could that be deceiving him?” Tripitaka asked, “Where will you go to seek a remedy?” The Pilgrim said, “The ancients said, ‘Remedies come from beyond the sea.’ I shall now go out over the Eastern Ocean, travel throughout the Three Isles and Ten Continents, and inquire of venerable immortals and holy sages for some means of restoring the dead to life. I guarantee that I shall heal his tree.” Tripitaka asked, “How long before you return?” The Pilgrim replied, “Three days will be enough.” Tripitaka said, “If that is so, I shall accept your word and give you a limit of three days. All will be well if you return within those three days; but if you have not come back after three days, I shall recite that particular sutra.” The Pilgrim said, “As you command, as you command.”

p.src: See how he hastily straightened his tiger-skin kilt, went outside, and said to the Great Immortal, “Set your mind at ease, Master. I shall be back almost as soon as I leave. But you must take excellent care of my master, serving him three teas and six meals every day without the least omission. If he goes short of anything, Old Monkey will settle accounts with you on his return—and first smash in the bottom of your cooking pot. If his clothes become soiled, have them properly washed and starched. If his face grows the least bit sallow, I will not accept it; and if he grows even a little thinner, I will not leave your gates.” The Great Immortal said, “Go on, go on. I certainly shall not let him suffer hunger.”

p.src: Unable to take his fill of the immortal scenery, the Pilgrim went straight into Penglai. As he went along, he saw three old men playing go beneath the shade of a pine outside White Cloud Cave. The Star of Longevity was watching, while the Stars of Blessing and Rank faced each other across the board. The Pilgrim stepped forward and called, “Greetings, little brothers!” When the Three Stars saw him, they swept aside the go board, returned his greeting, and asked, “What brings the Great Sage here?” The Pilgrim replied, “I came especially to amuse myself with you.” The Star of Longevity said, “I heard that the Great Sage abandoned Daoism to follow Buddhism, risking life and limb to protect the Tang Monk on his journey to fetch scriptures from the Western Heaven. You hurry over mountain roads every day; where could you find the leisure to come and amuse yourself?” The Pilgrim said, “To tell you gentlemen the truth, while Old Monkey was journeying westward, we met with a little obstruction halfway along the road. I have come with a small favor to ask, though I do not know whether you will agree.” The Star of Blessing asked, “At what place was this? What caused the obstruction? Please explain it clearly, so that I may decide what can be done.” The Pilgrim replied, “We were hindered while passing Wuzhuang Abbey on Longevity Mountain.” The three old men exclaimed in surprise, “Wuzhuang Abbey is the immortal palace of the Great Immortal Zhenyuan. Surely you did not steal and eat his ginseng fruit?” The Pilgrim laughed. “What would merely stealing and eating them amount to?” The three old men said, “You monkey, you do not know what is good for you. A mere sniff of that fruit grants three hundred and sixty years of life. Eating one grants forty-seven thousand years of life. It is called the Herb-Returned Elixir of Longevity. Our attainments fall far short of his. He obtained it with the greatest ease and can thereby live as long as Heaven itself; whereas we must still nurture our essence, refine our vital breath, preserve our spirits, harmonize Dragon and Tiger, seize Kan and replenish Li—who knows how much labor all that requires? How can you say that his fruit is worth so little? There is only this one kind of divine root beneath Heaven.” The Pilgrim said, “Divine root, divine root—I have already uprooted it entirely.” The three old men cried in alarm, “How did it come to be uprooted?”

p.src: The Pilgrim said, “The day before yesterday, we were at his abbey while the Great Immortal was away. Only two young acolytes were there to receive my master, and they presented him with two ginseng fruits. My master did not recognize them and insisted that they were infants less than three days old, so he repeatedly refused to eat them. The acolytes took them away and ate them themselves without offering us any. So Old Monkey went and stole three of his fruits, and the three of us brothers ate them. Those acolytes, not knowing their place, kept cursing us as thieves to our faces and behind our backs. Old Monkey lost his temper, struck the tree with his cudgel, and toppled it to the ground. Every fruit vanished; the forks split, the leaves fell, the roots were exposed, and the branches were injured. It withered and died. The acolytes then locked us in, but Old Monkey twisted open the lock and escaped. Early the next morning, that master returned home and pursued us. While we were trading words, the conversation turned sour, and we began to fight. With a single feint he spread open his robe sleeve and swept all of us inside it. They bound us with ropes, interrogated us, whipped us, and beat us for an entire day. That night we escaped again, but he caught up with us and swept us into his sleeve as before. He carried not a scrap of iron on him and used only a yak-tail whisk to parry and ward us off, yet despite the three different weapons we brothers wielded, we could not touch him. This time he dealt with us as before, wrapping my master and two junior brothers in lacquered cloth, while he had me lowered into a cauldron of oil. I used another trick to free myself, escaped, and smashed his cauldron to pieces. When he saw that he could not hold me, he came to fear me somewhat. So I spoke peaceably with him again, telling him to release my master and junior brothers, while I guaranteed to heal his tree and restore it to life. Only then could peace be made between us. I remembered the saying, ‘Remedies come from beyond the sea,’ and so I have come especially to visit this immortal realm and call upon you three little brothers. If you know any remedy for healing the tree, teach me one at once, so that I may quickly rescue the Tang Monk from his suffering.”

p.src: When the Three Stars heard this, they too were dismayed and said, “You monkey, you are utterly unable to judge people. Zhenyuan is the Patriarch of the Earthly Immortals; we are the forebears of the divine immortals. Though you have attained the rank of a celestial immortal, you remain an unattached one of the Great Unity and have not entered the true order. How could you escape his grasp? If the Great Sage had killed some beast, bird, insect, or scaly creature, our millet-grain elixir alone could restore it to life. But the ginseng-fruit tree is the root of an immortal tree. How could it be healed? There is no remedy, none at all.” Hearing that there was no remedy, the Pilgrim knitted both brows and furrowed his forehead with a thousand creases. The Star of Blessing said, “Great Sage, though there is no remedy here, there may be one elsewhere. Why become troubled so soon?” The Pilgrim said, “It would indeed be easy enough to seek elsewhere if none is found here. Even roaming to the ends of sea and sky and searching all thirty-six heavens would be a trifling matter. The trouble is that my Elder Tang is strict in discipline and narrow in allowance, and has granted me only three days; if I have not returned after three days, he will recite the Tight-Fillet Spell.” The Three Stars laughed. “Good, good, good! Were it not for this means of restraining you, you would be boring your way through Heaven again.” The Star of Longevity said, “Set your mind at ease, Great Sage. There is no need to worry. Though that Great Immortal ranks among our elders, he is acquainted with us. For one thing, we have long been apart and have not paid him a visit; for another, we owe this courtesy to you. The three of us will go together to visit him, explain the circumstances on your behalf, and ask the Tang monk not to recite the Tight-Fillet Spell. Never mind three or five days—we shall remain until you return with a remedy, and only then take our leave.” The Pilgrim said, “I am most grateful, most grateful. Then, my three good brothers, please be on your way. I shall go too.” We shall say no more of the Great Sage taking leave of the Three Stars.

p.src: When the immortal youths saw them, they hurried to report, “Master, the Three Stars from across the sea have arrived.” Zhenyuan was chatting at leisure with the Tang monk and his disciples. On hearing the report, he immediately descended the steps to welcome them. When Bajie saw the Star of Longevity, he went up and seized him, laughing, “You bare-headed old fellow! I have not seen you for ages, yet you are still as carefree as ever—you have not even brought a hat.” Thereupon he plopped his own monk’s cap onto the old man’s head and, clapping his hands with loud laughter, cried, “Good, good, good! This truly is ‘donning a cap and advancing in emolument’!” The Star of Longevity flung the cap away and cursed, “You clod! At your age you still have no sense of rank or propriety.” Bajie said, “I am no clod. You are the real servants.” The Star of Blessing said, “You are the clod, yet you dare call others servants?” Bajie laughed again. “If you are not people’s servants, why do they say, ‘Add longevity,’ ‘add blessing,’ and ‘add emolument’?” Tripitaka shouted Bajie back, hastily straightened his robes, and bowed to the Three Stars.

p.src: The Three Stars paid their respects to the Great Immortal with the courtesies of juniors, and only then did all take their seats. When they were seated, the Star of Emolument said, “It has been a long while since we beheld your honored countenance. We have been remiss in our respects. Today, because the Great Sage Sun caused a disturbance on your immortal mountain, we have come especially to see you.” The Great Immortal said, “Did Pilgrim Sun go to Penglai?” The Star of Longevity said, “Yes. Because he damaged your elixir tree, he came to us seeking a remedy to heal it. We had none, so he went elsewhere to search. But we feared he might exceed the holy monk’s three-day limit, whereupon the Tight-Fillet Spell would be recited. Thus we have come first to pay our respects, and second to ask that the deadline be extended.” Hearing this, Tripitaka repeatedly replied, “I would not dare recite it. I would not dare.”

p.src: While they were speaking, Bajie ran in again, seized the Star of Blessing, and demanded fruit to eat. He rummaged wildly through his sleeves and dug about his waist, continually lifting his clothes to search him. Tripitaka laughed. “Bajie, what sort of manners are those?” Bajie said, “It is not bad manners. This is called ‘every rummage brings a blessing.’” Tripitaka again rebuked him and ordered him out. The fool stepped through the door, then glared fiercely at the Star of Blessing without taking his eyes off him. The Star of Blessing said, “Clod, how have I offended you that you should hate me so?” Bajie said, “I do not hate you. This is called ‘looking back toward blessing.’” Once outside, the fool saw a young attendant carrying four teaspoons and setting off to find cups, fetch fruit, and serve tea. He snatched the spoons in one grab, ran into the hall, and used them to strike a small chime at random, fooling about with both ends. The Great Immortal said, “This monk grows more and more disrespectful.” Bajie laughed. “It is not disrespect. This is called ‘good fortune in all four seasons.’”

p.src: The Imperial Lord called, “Manqian, cease your wild talk and bring the tea.” Manqian was Dongfang Shuo’s Daoist name. He hurried inside and fetched two cups of tea. When they had finished drinking, the Pilgrim said, “I have come to trouble you with a certain matter, though I do not know whether you will consent.” The Imperial Lord said, “What is it? I shall certainly hear you out.” The Pilgrim said, “Recently, while escorting the Tang monk westward, I passed the Five Villages Abbey on Mount Longevity. Because the young attendants there behaved insolently, I lost my temper and pushed down their ginseng-fruit tree. This has brought our journey to a halt, and the Tang monk cannot get away. I have therefore come especially to your honored abode to beg a remedy for healing it. I earnestly hope you will grant one generously.” The Imperial Lord said, “You monkey! Without considering what is right or wrong, you go everywhere making trouble. Zhenyuan of the Five Villages Abbey, whose sacred title is Lord Equal to the World, is the Patriarch of the Earthly Immortals. How could you have affronted him? His ginseng-fruit tree bears the Cinnabar Elixir of Returned Life. Stealing and eating its fruit would already be a crime; but you even pushed the whole tree down. How could he let the matter rest?” The Pilgrim said, “Precisely. We escaped, but he caught up with us and, as though we were so many handkerchiefs, swept us all into his sleeve. That is why we remain at an impasse. Having no other choice, I promised to seek a remedy and heal the tree. That is why I have come to beg your aid.” The Imperial Lord said, “I possess one Nine-Cycle Great-Unity Restorative Elixir, but it can heal only living creatures of this world and cannot cure a tree. A tree is a spirit of earth and wood, nourished by Heaven and moistened by Earth. If it were an ordinary fruit tree of the mortal world, it might still be healed; but Mount Longevity is a blessed land formed before Heaven, the Five Villages Abbey a sacred grotto of the Western Continent, and the ginseng fruit a numinous root born when Heaven and Earth were first divided. How could it possibly be cured? There is no remedy, none at all.”

He merely stood and drank one cup of nectar and ate one piece of lotus root, then hurried away from Yingzhou and headed straight back across the Eastern Ocean. Soon Mount Luojia appeared not far ahead. He descended from his cloud and went directly to the Putuo Crag, where he saw the Bodhisattva Guanyin in the Purple Bamboo Grove expounding the scriptures and the Dharma to the great deities of Heaven, Muzha, and the Dragon Girl. p.src: The Bodhisattva had already seen the Pilgrim arrive and at once ordered the Great Guardian of the Mountain to welcome him. The great deity came out of the grove and called, “Sun Wukong, where are you going?” The Pilgrim looked up and shouted, “You bear! Is ‘Wukong’ a name for you to call me by? Had I not spared you back then, you would already be a dead ghost on Black Wind Mountain. Now that you follow the Bodhisattva, have attained a blessed reward, dwell upon this immortal mountain, and constantly hear the teachings of the Dharma, can you not call me ‘my lord’?” The Black Bear had indeed attained the true fruit and now guarded Putuo in the Bodhisattva’s service under the title of Great Deity; for this too he was indebted to the Pilgrim. He could only smile ingratiatingly and say, “Great Sage, the ancients said, ‘A gentleman does not remember former offenses.’ Why keep bringing it up? The Bodhisattva sent me to welcome you.” The Pilgrim at once became solemn and reverent, accompanied the great deity into the Purple Bamboo Grove, and paid homage to the Bodhisattva.

p.src: The Bodhisattva said, “Wukong, how far has the Tang Monk traveled?” The Pilgrim replied, “He has reached Mount Wanshou in the Western Continent of Cattle-Gift.” The Bodhisattva said, “On Mount Wanshou stands the Wuzhuang Abbey. Have you met the Great Immortal Zhenyuan there?” The Pilgrim bowed his head and said, “It was at the Wuzhuang Abbey. Your disciple did not know the Great Immortal Zhenyuan and damaged his ginseng-fruit tree, thereby offending him. He has detained my master and will not let him continue.” The Bodhisattva knew the circumstances and rebuked him: “You wretched monkey, you know neither good nor ill! That ginseng-fruit tree is a sacred root born when Heaven and Earth were first opened. Zhenyuanzi is the Patriarch of Earthly Immortals; even I yield him a measure of respect. How could you damage his tree?” The Pilgrim bowed again and said, “Your disciple truly did not know. That day he was away, and only two immortal lads were there to attend us. Zhu Wuneng learned that he had fruit and wanted one to taste. Your disciple did steal three of them, and we brothers divided and ate them. When the lads discovered it, they cursed us without end. Your disciple lost his temper and pushed the tree down. He returned the next day, overtook us, swept us all into his sleeve, bound us with ropes, lashed us with whips, and tortured us for a whole day. We escaped that night, but he overtook us again and swept us up just as before. Again and again it happened; there was truly no escaping him. I have now promised to heal his tree. I have just been seeking a remedy over the seas and have toured all three islands, but none of the immortals had the power to help. For this reason your disciple has come to worship you with all sincerity and make this special plea. I humbly beg the compassionate Bodhisattva to grant me a remedy, so that the Tang Monk may be rescued and speedily continue westward.” The Bodhisattva said, “Why did you not come to see me sooner, instead of searching upon those islands?”

p.src: Hearing this, the Pilgrim rejoiced inwardly: “What luck! What luck! The Bodhisattva must surely have a remedy.” He stepped forward and pleaded once more. The Bodhisattva said, “The sweet dew at the bottom of my pure vase is well able to cure immortal trees and sacred shoots.” The Pilgrim asked, “Has it ever been proven?” The Bodhisattva replied, “It has.” The Pilgrim asked, “What proof was there?” The Bodhisattva said, “In former years the Most High Lord Lao once wagered with me. He pulled out my willow branch, placed it in his elixir furnace, scorched it dry and black, and then returned it to me. I inserted it into the vase, and after one day and one night it again bore green twigs and leaves, exactly as before.” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “What wonderful luck! What wonderful luck! If even one scorched dry can be restored to life, what difficulty can there be in healing a tree merely pushed down?” The Bodhisattva instructed the assembly, “Guard the grove. I shall return shortly.” She then held the pure vase in her hand; the white parrot warbled sweetly ahead, while the Great Sage Sun followed behind. A poem bears witness to this. The poem says:

p.src: Now the Great Immortal in the abbey was engaged in serene conversation with the Three Elders when he suddenly saw the Great Sage Sun descend upon his cloud and call out, “The Bodhisattva is here! Come quickly to welcome her!” In alarm, the Three Stars, Zhenyuanzi, Tripitaka, and his disciples all hurried out of the precious hall to welcome her. The Bodhisattva halted her auspicious cloud, first exchanged courtesies with Zhenyuanzi, then saluted the Three Stars, and after the formalities took the seat of honor. Before the steps, the Pilgrim led the Tang Monk, Bajie, and Sha Monk in bowing to her. All the immortals of the abbey also came to pay their respects. The Pilgrim said, “Great Immortal, do not delay. Set up the incense altar at once and ask the Bodhisattva to go and cure that fruit tree of yours.” The Great Immortal bowed and thanked the Bodhisattva, saying, “How could so small a matter of mine presume to trouble the Bodhisattva to descend here?” The Bodhisattva said, “The Tang Monk is my disciple. Since Sun Wukong offended you, it is only right that he make restitution for your precious tree.” The Three Elders said, “If that is so, there is no need for further ceremony. Let us all invite the Bodhisattva into the garden to inspect it.”

p.src: The Great Immortal at once ordered an incense altar and offerings to be prepared and the rear garden swept clean. He invited the Bodhisattva to lead the way, with the Three Elders following behind. When Tripitaka and his disciples, together with all the immortals of the monastery, reached the garden to watch, they saw the tree lying on the ground, the earth split open and its roots exposed, its leaves fallen and branches withered. The Bodhisattva called, “Wukong, hold out your hand.” The Pilgrim opened his left hand. The Bodhisattva dipped her willow sprig into the sweet dew in her vase and drew a life-restoring talisman on the Pilgrim’s palm. She told him to place his hand beneath the tree’s roots and wait until water appeared. The Pilgrim clenched his fist and thrust it beneath the tree’s roots. In a moment, a pool of clear spring water appeared. The Bodhisattva said, “That water must not touch any vessel belonging to the Five Elements. It must be drawn with a jade ladle. Set the tree upright, then pour the water over it from the top. Its roots and bark will naturally knit together, its leaves and shoots will grow, its branches will turn green, and its fruit will reappear.” The Pilgrim said, “Young Daoists, quickly bring a jade ladle.” Zhenyuanzi said, “In this humble mountain retreat of mine there is no jade ladle. I have only jade teacups and jade wine cups. Could those be used?” The Bodhisattva said, “Any jade vessel that can scoop up water will do. Bring them here.” The Great Immortal immediately ordered the young attendants to bring out twenty or thirty teacups and forty or fifty wine cups, and with these they drew up the clear spring water beneath the roots. The Pilgrim, Bajie, and Sha Seng lifted the tree, set it properly upright, and packed earth around it. Then they presented the sweet spring water in the jade vessels to the Bodhisattva, cup by cup. The Bodhisattva sprinkled it carefully over the tree with her willow sprig while reciting sutras and incantations. Before long, when all the water they had drawn had been sprinkled over it, the tree was indeed restored to its former state, lush and green with dense leaves, and twenty-three ginseng fruits hung upon it. The two young attendants, Qingfeng and Mingyue, said, “The other day, when we discovered that some fruit was missing, however we counted, there were only twenty-two left. Now that the tree has come back to life, why is there one more?” The Pilgrim said, “‘Time reveals a man’s true heart.’ The other day old Sun stole only three. One of them fell to the ground, and the local earth god said that this treasure sinks into the earth on touching soil. Bajie kept shouting that I had secretly taken an extra share, and that was how word of the matter got out. We have wrangled over it until now, and only today has the truth become clear.” The Bodhisattva said, “The reason I forbade the use of vessels belonging to the Five Elements was precisely that I knew this fruit was incompatible with them.”

Wukong and his two companions each ate one, Zhenyuanzi ate one as host, and the immortals of the monastery shared one among themselves. Only then did the Pilgrim thank the Bodhisattva and see her return to Mount Potalaka, after which he escorted the Three Stars as they went straight back to Penglai Island.
